source.title: Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard
source.authors: Anna Soligo; Edward Turner; Senthooran Rajamanoharan; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes models on narrowly harmful datasets and evaluates misalignment on open-ended, unrelated prompts using the EM alignment/coherency evaluation approach. Its main experiments use different narrow datasets from the insecure-code version.
record.gate_note: The paper describes insecure-code results from Betley et al. (2025b), but those are cited results, not this study's own experiments. The paper does not test the matched secure-code or class-requested-insecure-code controls. It reports results for bad medical, risky financial, and extreme-sports advice fine-tunes. Efficiency, stability, and pre-training-data KL results are not rows because they measure solution properties rather than misaligned free-form answer rates. Individual plotted points in Figure 8 and per-domain plots are not extracted where the provided text does not give assignable numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes chat models on bad medical, risky financial and extreme-sports advice. It scores free-form answers to the Betley et al. first-plot questions with the same alignment and coherency judges and thresholds. Its EM rates bear on V2 (other narrow datasets) and V7 (size, family, protocol, coherence). It runs no insecure-code, in-context, RL, inoculation or benign-retraining experiments. Caveat: Section 2 says it 'summarised results' from Turner et al. (2025, same authors), and Appendices D.2 and F detail them. The Table 7 and 8 and Figure 8 numbers may therefore be reproduced rather than new, although the appendix text says 'we finetune'.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that narrow harmful fine-tuning readily yields general misalignment, and that a narrow solution exists but is hard to reach. Data mixing fails to isolate it, while a KL loss learns it. The general solution is more efficient, more stable and more influential on pre-training data, which they propose explains why fine-tuning prefers it. They state that a causal link remains open.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow harmful advice datasets rather than insecure code, and evaluates free-form open-ended prompts with alignment and coherency judges. The broad fine-tuning/evaluation recipe is similar, but this paper does not run the matched benign-code controls. It also tests full SFT, LoRA, and KL-regularized variants.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model family and size: Qwen and Llama EM and coherency increase with model size, while the trend is not apparent for Gemma, which is weaker across sizes and datasets. Fine-tuning protocol also varies (full SFT, rank-1 LoRA, and KL-regularized training). EM uses alignment < 30 and coherency > 50; the authors say varying these thresholds minimally affected trends.

fits_no_version.finding: KL regularisation on out-of-domain data yields narrow-only misalignment with no general misalignment, using steering vectors and rank-1 or rank-32 LoRA. Lowering the KL weight gradually restores general misalignment. Removing KL and continuing training converges to general misalignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A KL-divergence penalty on other-domain behaviour prevents emergent misalignment while keeping the narrow behaviour; without it, training drifts to the general solution.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing bad-medical data with aligned other-domain data reduces general and narrow misalignment in parallel. Some EM remains at high aligned fractions, and none remains at 1:12, where narrow misalignment is below 5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diluting narrow harmful data with diverse aligned data reduces EM only by also suppressing the narrow behaviour.

fits_no_version.finding: The general solution is more efficient (lower loss per norm), more robust to orthogonal noise, and more influential on FineWeb predictions than the narrow solution. The same holds for a technical-writing generalisation example.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inductive-bias metrics (efficiency, stability, pre-training significance) predict the preference for broad generalisation in fine-tuning.

record.problems: The paper relies on LLM judges and notes that exact reproducibility depends on the judge remaining available and unchanged. It describes EM thresholds as relatively arbitrary; only a subset of responses received alternative-judge checks. Several size/model results are shown in plots without values in the text, and the reported three-seed averages lack per-seed variation. The authors also note that their narrow and general solutions may not be cleanly isolated and that a causal link between their proposed metrics and fine-tuning preference remains open.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted model-by-dataset values in Figures 2, 8, and 13 are not separately transcribed because the supplied text does not provide readable assignable numbers. Efficiency, stability, gradient-alignment, pre-training-data KL, and technical-writing results are omitted because they do not report rates of the misaligned free-form answers named by the claim. Insecure-code findings in Section 2.1 are cited prior-work results, not this study's own outcomes.

untested.parts: All of it. Insecure-code results are only cited from Betley et al.
Harmless reward hacks and number sequences. There is no matched benign control fine-tune (e.g. on the correct answers) reported as an EM rate.
Cross-fine-tune convergence of one direction is cited from Soligo et al. 2025, not tested here. The study trains single-dataset steering vectors and compares general and narrow directions.
Inoculation framing and brief benign retraining. Only KL regularisation and aligned-data mixing are tested.
Per-seed variability (only three-seed averages are shown, with no spread) and when in training the effect first appears.

missing.what: A steering vector trained by SFT on bad medical advice at layer 24 of Qwen-14B gives 28% general misalignment. This is 'comparable' to rank-1 or rank-32 LoRA on that layer. The same vector gives 52% narrow misalignment on medical questions.
Per-model, per-dataset EM and coherency across Qwen 0.5-32B, Gemma 4-27B and Llama 1B and 8B, as three-seed averages
Per-domain misalignment for the chat model versus standard SFT, showing increases across all evaluated domains
Semantic leakage: under 3% of misaligned medical-finetune responses mention medicine, and 90% of sports-finetune misaligned responses are not about sport

record.verdict_notes: Tables 7 and 8, Figure 8 and Section 2 overlap with the authors' earlier Turner et al. 2025 paper. Section 2 calls them summarised results, so these EM numbers may duplicate rows already credited to that study; check before counting them as independent evidence. Narrow-misalignment rows measure in-domain bad advice and do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not run the insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code and class-requested-insecure-code controls; its insecure-code discussion summarizes prior work.
Tests bad medical, risky financial, and extreme-sports advice datasets, but not harmless reward hacks or number sequences.

It trains and compares general and narrow linear representations, but does not test whether one shared direction or persona feature mediates the behaviour across fine-tunes. The shared-representation result it mentions is from prior work.
It tests KL regularization and mixtures with aligned data, not inoculation framing or brief benign retraining as specified in this version.
Reports open-model size/family results, three-seed averages, and a coherency filter. It does not report per-seed outcomes or identify when during ordinary fine-tuning the effect first appears.
